title: Joshua 22:1–9
context: With the land given and rest secured, Joshua commends Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh for keeping their pledge (Numbers 32; Joshua 1), charges them to love and serve the LORD, blesses them, and sends them home across the Jordan.

verses.text: Then Joshua called the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh,
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua summons Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Arminian readers see a leader honoring the tribes who kept their promise to fight alongside their brothers west of the Jordan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Joshua acknowledging faithful service. The scene recalls the agreement recorded in Numbers 32 and Joshua 1, where these tribes pledged to help conquer the land.

verses.text: and said to them, “You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, and have listened to my voice in all that I commanded you.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua says, “You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you.” Arminian readers see genuine obedience recognized and commended, not dismissed as insignificant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see faithfulness praised as obedience to God’s word through Moses. Joshua’s commendation shows that the eastern tribes fulfilled their part of the covenant arrangement.

verses.text: You have not left your brothers these many days to this day, but have performed the duty of the commandment of the LORD your God.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua notes that they did not abandon their brothers but performed the LORD’s command. Arminian readers see loyalty to the community expressed through costly, sustained effort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see obedience to God shown in faithfulness to fellow Israelites. The long service of these tribes models solidarity within God’s people.

verses.text: Now the LORD your God has given rest to your brothers, as he spoke to them. Therefore now return and go to your tents, to the land of your possession, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua says the LORD has given rest, so they may return to the land Moses gave them beyond the Jordan. Arminian readers see their obligation fulfilled and their freedom to go home granted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s gift of rest marking the completion of their task. The return home is presented as the fruit of God’s faithfulness, not merely the end of a military campaign.

verses.text: Only take diligent heed to do the commandment and the law which Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, to love the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua urges them “to love the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him.” Arminian readers see an earnest call to continued faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the heart of covenant life summarized. The charge echoes Deuteronomy’s language of wholehearted love and service, applying it to tribes who will live at a distance from the sanctuary.

verses.text: So Joshua blessed them, and sent them away; and they went to their tents.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua blesses them and sends them home. Arminian readers see blessing as a gracious send-off that encourages the tribes to remain faithful in their own land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the leader’s blessing invoking God’s favor on those departing. The brief verse marks a peaceful parting that the following events will test.

verses.text: Now to the one half-tribe of Manasseh Moses had given inheritance in Bashan; but Joshua gave to the other half among their brothers beyond the Jordan westward. Moreover when Joshua sent them away to their tents, he blessed them,
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator explains the two halves of Manasseh, then notes Joshua blessed them again. Arminian readers see attention to the divided tribe, ensuring both parts are recognized as full members of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the explanatory note clarifying tribal arrangements. The repeated blessing emphasizes Joshua’s goodwill toward the eastern tribes.

verses.text: and spoke to them, saying, “Return with much wealth to your tents, with very much livestock, with silver, with gold, with bronze, with iron, and with very much clothing. Divide the plunder of your enemies with your brothers.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua says, “Return with much wealth to your tents,” and tells them to share the plunder with their brothers. Arminian readers see generosity expected as a response to God’s provision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s gifts meant to be shared within the community. The instruction to divide the plunder reinforces bonds between the tribes on both sides of the Jordan.

verses.text: The children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh returned, and departed from the children of Israel out of Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead, to the land of their possession, which they owned, according to the commandment of the LORD by Moses.
verses.arminianNotes: The eastern tribes leave Shiloh for Gilead, according to the LORD’s command through Moses. Arminian readers see their departure as orderly and obedient, not a break from Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see them acting within God’s arrangements. The reference to Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, sets up the coming question about worship and the altar.
